prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Two people who have never met can agree on a secret while a third person reads every word they exchange. The method was published in 1976 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, and it uses arithmetic that a school pupil can follow.

Call the two people Alice and Bob, and call the listener Eve. Alice and Bob can only talk over a line that Eve can hear in full. They want to finish with the same number, one that Eve cannot work out, so that they can use it as the key for scrambling their later messages. Before 1976 every method of secret writing needed the two sides to share a key in advance, which meant meeting in private or sending a courier. That is no use for a shopper and a website that connect for the first time and have a fraction of a second to sort things out.

The idea rests on a calculation that is quick to do and impractical to reverse, and mixing paint is a fair picture of it. Suppose Alice and Bob agree out loud on a yellow paint as the starting point. Alice secretly picks red and Bob secretly picks blue. Alice stirs her red into a jar of the yellow and sends the jar to Bob, and Bob stirs his blue into a jar of the yellow and sends it to Alice. Eve sees both jars, but nobody can separate mixed paint into its parts. Alice now stirs her own red into the jar she received, and Bob stirs his own blue into the jar he received. Both jars end up with yellow, red and blue in the same amounts, so both are the same colour. Eve holds only the yellow and red jar and the yellow and blue jar, and nothing she can add to them gives the colour that Alice and Bob hold.

Numbers can do the same job, and for that we need clock arithmetic. On a twelve-hour clock, six hours after nine o'clock is three o'clock, because the hands go round and start again at twelve. The rule is to divide by 12 and keep the remainder. Take a clock with 23 positions, where any number is replaced by its remainder after dividing by 23. A power such as 5 to the power 6 means six fives multiplied together, which is 15,625. Dividing 15,625 by 23 gives 679 with 8 left over, so on this clock 5 to the power 6 lands on 8. That direction is easy. The reverse question, which power of 5 lands on 8, has no formula. The only general approach is to try 5 to the power 1, then 2, then 3, and keep going until the right one turns up.

Here is the exchange. Alice and Bob agree in public on the clock size, 23, and the base, 5. Alice chooses a private number, 6, and works out 5 to the power 6 on the clock, which is 8. She sends 8 to Bob. Bob chooses a private number, 15. Five to the power 15 is 30,517,578,125, and the remainder after dividing by 23 is 19, so he sends 19 to Alice.

Next, Alice takes the 19 that Bob sent and raises it to her private power, 6. The result is 47,045,881, which leaves a remainder of 2 after division by 23. Bob takes the 8 that Alice sent and raises it to his private power, 15. The result is 35,184,372,088,832, which also leaves a remainder of 2. Both now hold the number 2, and neither has ever said it aloud.

The two answers match because of a rule about powers. Bob's 19 came from 5 to the power 15, and Alice's 8 came from 5 to the power 6. Alice raised Bob's number to the power 6, which gives 5 to the power 15 times 6, or 5 to the power 90. Bob raised Alice's number to the power 15, which gives 5 to the power 6 times 15, which is also 5 to the power 90. Multiplying 15 by 6 gives the same result as multiplying 6 by 15, so both roads end at the same place. Reducing to remainders along the way does not disturb this, because the remainder of a product depends only on the remainders of the numbers being multiplied.

Eve has heard 23, 5, 8 and 19. She has not heard 6 or 15. With numbers this small she could try the powers of 5 in order, find that the sixth gives 8, and then repeat Alice's last step to get 2. That would take her seconds, so the example only demonstrates the steps. Real systems use a clock whose size is a prime number of at least 2,048 binary digits, which is a number with about 617 decimal digits. The private numbers are of similar size. A computer can still raise a number to such a power quickly, because it squares the number repeatedly and combines the results, which takes a few thousand multiplications. Eve, though, faces a search through an astronomical number of possible powers. Methods faster than trying every power are known, but the fastest would still need far more computing than exists. It is my reading of the evidence, and the general view among cryptographers, that no quick method will be found, but nobody has proved that. The confidence comes from decades of failed attempts to find one.

There is a limit to what the exchange gives. It protects against someone who only listens. If Eve can also alter messages, she can pretend to be Bob when she talks to Alice and pretend to be Alice when she talks to Bob. She would then agree one secret with each of them and pass messages between the two, reading all of them on the way. The exchange has no way of telling Alice who is on the other end. Websites deal with this by presenting a certificate, which is a statement that a named organisation holds a particular public number, signed by an authority that the browser already trusts. The padlock in a browser is a sign that this check has passed.

The same kind of one-way calculation also allows a different tool, which is called public-key encryption. In 1977 Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman described a version known as RSA. Multiplying two primes is easy, since 3 times 7 is 21, but given only a large product it is hard to find the primes that made it. Bob chooses two large primes, keeps them private, and publishes their product. Anyone can use the published number to lock a message so that it is readable only to someone who knows the primes. It works like a padlock that Bob leaves open in a public place. Anyone can snap it shut on a box, and only Bob has the key to open it again. Researchers at the British agency GCHQ, among them Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson, had reached these ideas in the early 1970s, but their work stayed secret until 1997.

In daily use the two methods work together. Public-key calculations are slow compared with ordinary scrambling methods such as AES, so they are used only to set up a shared key. Once your browser and a website have agreed on that number, in the way shown above and with far larger figures, they switch to the faster method and use the shared number as its key. Eve sees all of it and learns nothing she can use.
